NVIDIA is bringing together a new Windows platform for local AI, creative work, and gaming under the name RTX Spark. The first laptops are expected to be available on October 16, 2026; compact desktop PCs are announced for November. At its core is a Blackwell graphics processor connected to a Grace CPU and up to 128 GB of shared memory. NVIDIA also promises one petaflop of AI computing performance in FP4 format, extensive CUDA compatibility, and a gaming offering with DLSS, ray tracing, and Reflex. This sounds like an unusually versatile package, but so far it is primarily a manufacturer’s proposal: prices, independent benchmarks, reliable battery life figures, and complete measurement conditions are not yet available.

The product overview released today does, however, make clearer what lies behind the initially rather generous “up to” figures. NVIDIA lists two laptop configurations: one with 6,144 GPU cores and 20 Grace CPU cores, and one with 5,120 GPU cores and 18 CPU cores. For both, the company specifies a TDP range of 45 to 80 watts; depending on the configuration, the upper limits for Unified Memory are 128 or 64 GB of LPDDR5X. This is a relevant clarification, but it does not replace information on prices, specific devices, cooling solutions, or sustained performance. The advertised all-day battery life remains unquantified, as does the claim that the chip is particularly energy-efficient.

NVIDIA lists the ASUS ProArt P16, Dell XPS 16, HP OmniBook Ultra 16, Lenovo Pro 9n, Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, and MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+ as laptop partners. The platform is also expected to appear in compact desktops from various manufacturers, including Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP, Lenovo, and MSI. Pre-orders have been announced, but specific prices and complete configurations for the individual devices are not yet available. Technical details on memory bandwidth, the power consumption of individual components, and thermal limits are also insufficient to assess actual sustained performance.

### Local AI: attractive, provided memory and software cooperate

NVIDIA positions RTX Spark as a computer on which AI models and agents can run directly on the user’s own device. An agent is more than a chat window: it can break tasks into multiple steps, call programs and tools, and automate workflows. NVIDIA cites fast iteration, no ongoing API costs per request, and data that stays on the user’s own computer as advantages of local execution. For larger tasks, work can be moved to the cloud without changing the code written for it. This is a plausible usage concept, but in practice, privacy, costs, and performance depend just as much on the software, model, and specific configuration as on the hardware. According to NVIDIA, up to 128 GB of Unified Memory will support models with up to 120 billion parameters and a context window of one million tokens. Unified Memory refers to a shared memory area for the CPU and GPU. This can help with large models because multiple separate memory pools do not need to be populated; however, by itself, it says nothing about memory bandwidth or the speed of a specific inference workload. The advertised one-petaflop FP4 performance refers to a lower numerical precision that can make AI computations more efficient, but it cannot readily be equated with performance at higher precision or with an independent application test.

NVIDIA names CUDA, TensorRT, and NVFP4 as development and inference tools. CUDA is the widely used NVIDIA platform through which software runs computing tasks on GPUs; TensorRT optimizes models for inference, while NVFP4 refers to an NVIDIA implementation of computations using particularly compact FP4 numerical precision. NVIDIA promises that applications developed on RTX Spark will also run unchanged on other NVIDIA GPUs. For developers, this shared software foundation is a key part of the offering; whether a project can actually run without modifications nevertheless depends on the libraries, drivers, and functions used. At launch, agent programs such as GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi, and WorkBuddy are intended to simplify setup, suggest suitable local models, and mediate between local operation and cloud services. NVIDIA Switchyard is intended as an open-source library for routing between these models; Hermes is expected to integrate it later in October, while Perplexity Computer and GitHub Copilot use their own routing solutions, according to NVIDIA. Such hybrid approaches can use local computing power for routine tasks and switch to cloud models when more capacity is needed. They do not automatically make execution free or entirely local, however.

For security, NVIDIA cites OpenShell and Microsoft Execution Containers, or MXC. MXC is intended to isolate agents at the operating system level and make them controllable; according to the manufacturer, OpenShell simplifies integration and adds credential protection and security monitoring. OpenClaw and GitHub Copilot are already expected to support MXC, while Hermes Agent is expected to add the controls by the end of October. Microsoft also describes the platform as a foundation for managing agent permissions and behavior in the Windows environment. The effectiveness of these safeguards in everyday use remains to be demonstrated through specific applications and security assessments.

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B is due to be released on October 15. According to NVIDIA, the Mixture-of-Experts model comprises 74 billion parameters but activates nine billion of them per processing step. With 2-bit quantization and quantization-aware training, it is intended to fit in 24 GB of memory. This combination targets agents that program, research, or use tools locally; the claim that the model is faster than many widely used dense models while also being more capable than comparable MoE models comes from NVIDIA and is not supported by independent comparative tests. The named runtime environments are llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth, and LM Studio. NVIDIA describes the model, including its training data, weights, and recipes, as open source. A smaller Nemotron model, Bolt E4B 4GB, is announced for October 23. It is intended to serve as the third generation of a Small Language Model for NVIDIA ACE in game characters and respond to natural conversations, tool use, and the current game state. NVIDIA highlights its low memory requirements and short response times, but comparative data is also lacking here. As earlier examples, the company cites a public test featuring AI teammates in PUBG and a voice-reactive companion in the game Aniimo.

The Llama Windows app is intended to make models from the Hugging Face Hub discoverable and enable their local use through llama.cpp without the command line. According to NVIDIA, llama.cpp is also expanding its support for decision models, which are intended to help agents with classification and choosing the next step. However, the claimed up-to-200-times-faster decision-making compared with traditional agents is not a reliable basis for comparison without specified test tasks and measurement conditions. NVIDIA PAIR, a tool for connecting compatible computers on a local network, is expected to leave beta, support llama.cpp, and distribute inference workloads across multiple systems. The software is announced for Windows, Linux, and macOS; direct model downloads from Hugging Face and configurable inference settings are among the stated new features.

Developer tools for Windows on Arm are also part of the initiative. NVIDIA and Microsoft cite a native PyTorch CUDA build, a native Python build with Python 3.15, and a Conda installer with more than 2,000 packages. Availability is already in place for 97 percent of the 15,000 most important Python wheels; NVIDIA intends to work with the community on the remaining packages. CUDA, PyTorch, and the CUDA libraries are expected to be available on RTX Spark. In addition, NVIDIA is providing so-called Skills for CUDA-X tools, intended to teach agents how to work with development libraries. The MCP interfaces for NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, and RTX Remix also aim to connect agents with specific programs and functions.

### Creative software, video, and the NVIDIA App

For selected Adobe applications, NVIDIA promises up to twice the performance. Photoshop is set to gain GPU-accelerated compositing as well as improvements to Remove Tool and effects such as Light Leaks. In Premiere, the focus is on playback, rendering, color correction, and AI features such as Enhance Speech and Object Mask; Substance 3D Painter is expected to accelerate high-resolution mesh baking as well as opening, saving, and exporting large projects, among other tasks. The optimizations for Photoshop and Premiere are initially expected to be available in beta, with updates for Substance 3D to follow. Without details on the tested versions, projects, and systems, “up to 2x” remains a manufacturer claim, not a basis for a purchase recommendation.

NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 is expected to run natively on RTX Spark and add Video Super Resolution, Frame Generation, new Studio Voice profiles, and an offline file processor. Unlike real-time effects, a file can be processed afterward, which according to NVIDIA should allow certain effects to be delivered at higher quality. A new MCP server and a Skill are intended to let agents control Broadcast settings and process files. ComfyUI is getting RTX Video nodes for Frame Generation and HDR, as well as EXR export. As an example, NVIDIA cites converting a 1080p SDR clip at 30 frames per second to 60 frames per second and HDR, before exporting the result as EXR for color correction. These are workflow examples, not image-quality measurements.

In Blender 5.3, DLSS Ray Reconstruction is expected to become available in November as beta support for RTX Spark. The technology is intended to improve ray-tracing results in the viewport and make interactive navigation easier. For video editing and camera workflows, NVIDIA also promotes hardware encoding and decoding for HEVC, H.264, and AV1, as well as direct processing of 4:2:2 camera footage. RTX Video is intended to sharpen footage, while Broadcast processes camera and microphone input in real time. For local image and video generation, NVIDIA emphasizes that no subscriptions, per-prompt fees, or queues are required, provided the models actually run locally on the device.

The NVIDIA App brings together drivers, game and GPU settings, recording, performance indicators, and access to other applications. Game Ready Drivers are intended to optimize games on their release day, while Studio Drivers are aimed at creative software. The GPU Control Center lets users manage graphics settings and use DLSS overrides to enable newer models in supported games. Smooth Motion is intended to generate additional intermediate frames on GeForce RTX 40 and 50 GPUs. NVIDIA also offers cloud-based recommendations for graphics settings based on the GPU, CPU, and display, as well as automatic GPU tuning. No independent assessment of the performance impact or recommendations is available.

With ShadowPlay, users can save screenshots, gameplay footage, and the previous 30 seconds using Instant Replay. For manual recording, NVIDIA specifies up to 8K HDR at 30 frames per second or 4K HDR at 120 frames per second; RTX 40 GPUs are expected to support AV1 recording. The app also displays FPS, 1% lows, GPU and CPU utilization, as well as PC and system latency, and integrates Reflex Analyzer. Freestyle is intended to support more than 1,200 games with real-time filters, including RTX Dynamic Vibrance for adjusting color presentation and RTX HDR for adding HDR output in supported DirectX or Vulkan games.
